US bombers pulled from RAF Fairford in face of ‘some threats’, says Trump
Donald Trump says there were “some threats” that led the United States to pull bombers from a UK base.
The US president said the military aircraft “didn’t fly out by accident” from RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire.
Earlier, US secretary of state Marco Rubio had sought to play down the withdrawal of the planes after suggestions the move was linked to security concerns.
The top diplomat would not link the departure of the jets to a recent suspected terror plot targeting the base.
But asked as he left the White House on Monday if the planes had been moved in response to a threat, Mr Trump said: “Yeah, I think we can say that. They didn’t fly out by accident.
“No, but there were some threats and rather than tempting the enemy, we’ll capture the enemy and beat the enemy.
“But why should we keep them there? So we moved them around a little bit, not very far.”

sources.news_title: America’s bomber withdrawal points to wider UK-US friction
sources.text:
America’s bomber withdrawal points to wider UK-US friction
The Pentagon’s decision to relocate B-1 bombers from the British air base comes after months of frustration in the Trump administration over Britain’s defense spending.
LONDON — Britain and the U.S. sought to ease friction Monday after American bombers were suddenly moved amid major security concerns at the base that hosted U.S. aircraft used to strike Iran.
The U.S. move is the latest stumbling block in the special relationship between the allies and underscores reservations in Donald Trump’s administration about how the U.K. is handling its defense and security commitments.
The Pentagon confirmed on Sunday that it had removed all B-1 bombers from the RAF Fairford air base — where they were deployed to conduct what have been termed as "defensive" strikes against Iran — and sent them back to their home stations in America.
Advertisement
Trump went further, telling journalists Monday evening: "We had an idea that there might be a threat, and why would I leave them there? ... If we're going to be threatened we're just going to move them, and that sort of alleviates that."
It comes as Britain's counter-terrorism agencies investigate a suspected terror plot against the air base, which the U.K. government believes involves Tehran.
Trump on Monday added: "We actually know the people that made the threat, and they've got themselves a big problem," adding in response to a follow-up question: "They would be linked to Iran."
He later said that he believes the U.K. is still a safe place for U.S. forces.
Downing Street had earlier insisted that the base was safe, but refused to comment directly on America’s decision to remove the bombers from the area.
The move comes as the Trump administration has grown increasingly frustrated with the U.K.’s defense spending and the White House's continuing anger that the U.K. didn’t send warships to the Middle East to help with the American blockade of Iranian shipping.
Advertisement
Something deeper is wrong
London has yet to outline a path to meet the NATO standard of spending 3.5% of GDP on defense by 2035 — up from its current level of around 2.7%. It has also been shut out of a subgroup within the alliance convened by Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby. The group is slated to meet again in Poland some time later this month.
Late last month, Colby hinted at that frustration with London, saying the countries' long history will continue to bind them, but the British government needs to make the case to its people for spending more on defense.
“There's this incredible legacy, and that's what we want to rekindle,” Colby said. “Exactly how you convince the British people [to spend more on defense] I would not presume to say, but … there's probably sort of a degree of reconciliation between what the U.K. wants to be doing, what it spends, and what it spends on, because you know a modern military is not cheap.”
The U.S. is also conducting a sweeping review of its posture in European NATO countries — including the U.K. — which will determine the number of American troops and military assets on the continent.
Sophia Gaston, a senior national security researcher at King’s College London, said: “The Trump administration is undeniably sensitive to the costs of the Iran conflict as they head into the midterms next month, so their caution is understandable.
An armored vehicle is seen at RAF Fairford on Sept. 28, 2026. | Ben Stansall/AFP via Getty Images
“It’s also hard not to, at some level, perceive a degree of uncertainty about the capacity of the British services to currently prevent such an attack. That partly reflects the innate challenge drones and other aspects of modern warfare pose to the sitting ducks of expensive kit.
Advertisement
“But it also speaks to the American wariness towards the pressured state of Britain’s military capabilities. Not only does Washington no longer wish to be solely responsible for allies’ protection, its expectations for the security allies offer its bases has also increased.”
Trump on Monday praised his relationship with new U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham. He said: "He's liberal, very liberal, but I hear he's going to open up North Sea oil if he does that in Aberdeen. If he does that, you're going to have a rich country. If he doesn't, you're going to have a bankrupt country."
Britain’s security concerns
In May, the U.K. raised its terrorism threat level to “severe” — meaning a terrorist attack is highly likely — after its MI5 security service said the U.K. had been “experiencing a gradual increase in terrorist threats for some time” including from hostile states like Iran.
In Britain, police and the security services are dealing with a three-fold threat from Iran-backed groups: attacks against Iranian dissidents, attacks against the country’s Jewish population, and the targeting of U.S. assets such as those used for strikes against Tehran.
Counter Terrorism Policing is currently investigating potential Iranian state involvement in a major incident at RAF Fairford on Sept. 27, when police were alerted to three suspicious vehicles near the base.
Six men — including a British-Iranian national — have so far been arrested on suspicion of terror offenses. All have subsequently been released on bail while police continue their investigation.
Advertisement
US strike capability
Though the Pentagon stressed that bombers remain “ready to deliver precision global strike capabilities” — including from the U.S. mainland — removing them would make any further American strikes on Iran more complex, since the bombers would have to double their flight path from the continental U.S. to the Middle East.
There is a fresh U.S. buildup in the region, with a third aircraft carrier currently steaming across the Pacific along with several large amphibious ships carrying 2,500 Marines, joining the 2,500 already at sea in the Middle East, giving President Donald Trump more options should he restart the bombing campaign after the U.S. midterm elections in early November.
Christoph Bergs, a research analyst at the RUSI defense think tank, said: “The basing of US B-1 bombers at RAF Fairford for operational employment against Iran was based on the UK stipulation that these were only used for defensive strikes. This likely included a more modest targeting list. Their withdrawal reduces the capacity to quickly surge sorties against Iran, reducing the threat level somewhat.”
The Pentagon declined to comment on whether it will, or is considering, the removal of other aircraft from British bases used to support operations against Iran.
This article has been updated with comments from Donald Trump.

sources.news_title: B-1 bombers leave UK airbase amid fears of possible attack by Iran
sources.text:
The US military has withdrawn its entire contingent of B-1B Lancer bombers from RAF Fairford in the UK following fresh Iran-related security concerns surrounding the strategic airbase.
All US long-range bombers based at the Gloucestershire facility returned to their home stations in the US on Sunday, October 4. At least a dozen B-1B Lancers are believed to have been stationed there before their departure.
The move comes as British counter-terrorism police investigate suspicious activity near the Royal Air Force station and amid reports that US commanders received new information about a possible threat involving Iran.
A Pentagon official confirmed that all the bombers had been withdrawn. Aircraft-tracking services recorded the B-1s leaving the base. “We can acknowledge now that all US bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have re-deployed to their home stations in the United States,” the Pentagon representative told CNN.
Security fears on the rise
The aircraft reportedly departed quickly enough that aerial refueling tankers were still being organized to support their flights across the Atlantic. According to the BBC, the withdrawal follows an incident near RAF Fairford on Sunday, September 27. At the time, police were alerted to three suspicious vehicles traveling near the installation.
More from Military
See All
Five UK-citizens, aged between 23 and 25, were initially detained on suspicion of explosives-related offenses. Police subsequently investigated them on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act before releasing them on bail.
Authorities later arrested a sixth suspect, a 25-year-old British-Iranian national, in London. He was also released on bail as the investigation continued. UK officials have pointed to an elevated threat from Iran but have not publicly linked Tehran to the RAF Fairford incident. Iran, however, has denied involvement.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham indicated that Iran may have played a role in the incident. “We will say more in due course, but we can confirm our belief that we believe Iran to have played a part,” he said. Reports stated that the Pentagon ordered the move at an operational military level rather than through a political decision.
Keeping US bombers safe
RAF Fairford is a key forward operating base for the US Air Force in Europe. It has hosted B-1B Lancers and B-52 Stratofortress bombers, and supported numerous US operations across Europe and the Middle East.
Ezra Cohen, a former defense official under Trump’s first administration, backed the decision to move the bombers from the base. “The B-1 bomber is a strategic asset, and we’re going to take steps to protect it, from all sorts of threats,” Cohen pointed out.
Meanwhile, during a Fox News interview on September 29, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, acknowledged possible foreign involvement in the alleged plot. He, however, denied identifying who may have been responsible. “It’s one that clearly involved the hands of a foreign actor, I won’t get into great detail about that yet,” he said.
Though no longer in production, the supersonic B-1B is one of the US Air Force’s most powerful long-range bombers. The jet can exceed 900 miles per hour (mph) and carry up to 75,000 pounds of conventional weapons. This gives it the largest conventional payload capacity in the US Air Force fleet.

“It’s reared its ugly head under President Trump because of the war in Iran,” Sen. John Kennedy, R-Louisiana, said. “Once we settle the war in Iran, those prices will come down.”

Senior Trump administration officials gathered at Camp David on Friday for hours of high-level discussions about the war with Iran and the rapidly escalating conflict between Iran-backed Houthi forces and the Saudi-backed government in Yemen.
The previously unannounced meeting brought together some of President Donald Trump’s most senior national security advisers as the administration weighs its next steps in two increasingly interconnected Middle East conflicts.
Vice President JD Vance chaired the session, according to Axios.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, CIA Director John Ratcliffe, Middle East envoy Steve Witkoff and Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman Gen. Dan Caine were among those attending, CBS News reported.
Trump was not reported to have attended the Camp David meeting. Officials discussed possible next steps in the Iran war as well as whether and how the United States should support a major Saudi-backed campaign against the Houthis in Yemen.
The meeting took on additional significance because of its timing.
The U.S. military evacuated a dozen B-1 bombers from the RAF Fairford airbase in the UK over the weekend, the Pentagon said.
A U.S. official said the base was under threat of attack by Iran.
Rubio told reporters on Monday that there are “regular rotations” of U.S. Air Force assets around the world and that the movement of the bombers was not directly tied to the Iranian threat.
“We have confidence in the security of all of our bases. All of our bases could be threatened theoretically at any moment and that is why there is so much security built around them,” he said.
Rubio said the U.S. has been working closely with the British government on an investigation into the threat “and they couldn’t be more cooperative.”
British security forces last week arrested several dual British-Iranian citizens suspected of planning an attack on the base.
Saudi Arabia has been pressing Washington for additional military assistance as Yemen’s internationally recognized government attempts to retake territory controlled by the Houthis.

For now, the Trump administration has stopped short of approving American combat operations.
U.S. officials said Washington is providing intelligence and targeting assistance to Saudi and Yemeni forces but is not currently conducting direct strikes against the Houthis as part of the new offensive.
One official said that position could change depending on developments on the battlefield.

They have launched missiles and drones at Saudi targets, including energy facilities, while fighting Saudi-backed Yemeni forces for control of strategically important territory.
Yemen’s internationally recognized government announced Sunday that it was launching a major operation aimed at retaking Houthi-held areas.
Tens of thousands of Yemeni government troops are participating, while Saudi Arabia is providing extensive air support.
Rashad al-Alimi, head of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council, said the objective is ultimately to regain territory controlled by the Houthis, including the capital, Sanaa.
Trump has repeatedly indicated that he wants the Iran conflict concluded but has also warned Tehran that additional American military action remains possible.
Speaking Friday night at a rally in Mobile, Alabama, Trump predicted the war would end “very soon,” suggesting it could happen shortly after the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
“It’s gonna end very soon, probably right after the election,” Trump said.
Trump argued that the United States had already inflicted such extensive damage on Iran’s military and infrastructure that Washington could end its operations immediately without allowing Tehran to quickly restore its previous capabilities.
“We could leave tomorrow and it would take them years to rebuild from what we did to them,” Trump said. “They shoulda negotiated.”
Trump specifically pointed to earlier B-2 bomber strikes against Iranian nuclear facilities.
“The B-2 bombers took ’em out,” Trump said.
Diplomatic efforts have continued alongside the fighting, but recent negotiations have produced little visible progress.
Rubio last week ordered an Iranian delegation in New York for the United Nations General Assembly to leave the United States after U.S. officials concluded that discussions had stalled.
Two remaining members subsequently departed after the State Department demanded that they leave, although Tehran disputed Washington’s characterization of the episode.

A Pentagon official confirmed that roughly a dozen B-1 bombers were returned to their US home stations on Sunday.
Washington gave no reason, but British sources said the decision was linked to the 27 September incident, when police responded to three “suspicious vehicles” near the base.
Six men were arrested in connection with suspected terror offences and later released on bail.
US officials reportedly received fresh intelligence about a possible Iran-backed plot, prompting commanders to act quickly.
The timing matters. RAF Fairford has long served as a forward base for US bombers operating toward the Middle East.
The B-1s can carry precision-guided weapons and missiles, making the base a valuable launch point.

Tehran has also warned that bases used against Iran could become targets.
The Pentagon insists its aircraft can still conduct missions “anywhere, anytime” from the continental US.
So, is this simply an operational precaution, or does pulling the bombers signal a deeper security concern?
Either way, RAF Fairford suddenly looks a lot less busy and potentially a lot more complicated.

sources.text:
The US on Sunday confirmed that it has withdrawn all B-1 bombers from the British air base of RAF Fairford, with officials telling US media that the move was linked to “new threats.”
Police were called to the base in southwest England on Sept. 27 after a local farmer reported a group of men with several vans engaged in “suspicious” activity.
The scare prompted a counterterrorism probe and forced evacuations at 85 homes near the air base, which was used by the US to launch strikes on Iran.
Photo: AFP
Investigators did not find any explosives in the vans, but “a quantity of petrol was recovered,” counterterrorism police said.
A statement from a Pentagon official on Sunday said “we can acknowledge now that all US bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have redeployed to their home stations in the United States.”
“Operational security precluded us from confirming the movement of our assets and forces in real-time,” it said.
An unidentified US official told CNN that the bombers were moved after “an unspecified new threat,” with the source calling the latest threat a “real world incident.”
It was unusual to move the bombers back to their home stations instead of deploying them to another base in the region, the official reportedly said.
Two US officials told the New York Times that the bombers were moved after commanders received new threats about an Iran-backed plot against the base.
One US official said the new information was part of the same threat warnings that surfaced three weeks ago, but the situation became urgent in the past 24 hours, the Times reported.
Speculation about the motives behind the incident ranged from terror threat to fuel thievery, as energy prices in the UK hit record highs this week.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said there were “strong indications that Iran played a part” in the incident, a charge rejected by Tehran.
Six London-based Britons arrested in the incident, including a UK-Iranian dual national, all men in their mid-20s, were released on bail, drawing rebuke from Washington.
“I wouldn’t have done that,” US President Donald Trump told reporters, as US Secretary of State Marco Rubio alleged a “foreign actor” was involved.
Iran’s embassy in London said it “categorically rejects and strongly condemns” speculation that Tehran was involved.

sources.text:
(The Center Square) – U.S. bombers being moved back to the U.S. from the UK are the latest in American military assets being shifted in Europe, as Secretary of War Pete Hegseth told The Center Square that he expects more troops to be moved back to the Western Hemisphere from Europe.
The Pentagon confirmed all the bombers have been moved from the Royal Air Force Base in Fairford, UK, following an alleged foiled attack on the base last weekend.
The move comes hours after Hegseth told The Center Square the U.S. is expanding its “footprint in Central and South America with partners.”
The secretary added that as relationships with Central and South American countries progress, the U.S. wants “more burden sharing in Europe,” while focusing more on the U.S. and its own backyard.
“As we do that, a lot of those capabilities are going to move elsewhere, either back home to the big, beautiful base that we’re going to build…or to a different posture in the Western Hemisphere as we can get after these designated terrorist organizations. We are at war with the drug cartels, with DTOs,” Hegseth told The Center Square. The president’s been clear about that, so we’re going to posture and base as necessary to ensure that we have our foot on the pedal and are taking the fight to those ISIS and Al Qaeda in our hemisphere.”
The potential shift comes as the Trump administration has sought to dominate power in the Western Hemisphere, being called the Donroe Doctrine, a play on the Monroe Doctrine.
In the past year, there has been a major political shift in Central and South America, as nations have begun to move away from Marxist-aligned leadership and toward open-market candidates.
Last week, The Center Square asked President Donald Trump whether he had plans to build a military base in South America, including Venezuela, as there are currently no military bases in the region.
Trump appeared to leave the door open for the possibility of military bases in Venezuela or South America.
“We’re looking at doing a lot of things. We’re getting along very well, as you know. And Venezuela has been a great situation,” the president told The Center Square. “We’re taking a lot of oil, and we have a great relationship. And Venezuela’s making a lot of money, and so are we. We’re going to start filling up our national strategic reserves with the Venezuelan oil for very little money, and it’s going to be great.”
The potential shifts come as the U.S. reached an agreement to build two bases in Greenland.
The president’s influence in South America has been felt after a group of Trump-backed candidates on the continent won elections, further strengthening his standing in the region.
Following the siege and arrest of Venezuela’s former dictator, Nicolas Maduro, the U.S. has seized an opportunity to build relations and take charge of one of the world’s oil markets.
Up until the arrest of Maduro and his wife at the start of the year, Venezuela built relationships with China, Russia, and Iran, placing some of America’s greatest adversaries at its back door. In addition to keeping global adversaries in check, the Trump administration has been targeting narco terrorists around the Caribbean and South America for over a year.
In 2022, Venezuela hosted military drills with countries including Russia, China and Iran.
The Trump administration has already confirmed a drawdown of American troops in parts of Western Europe, specifically Germany, while floating the idea of moving additional troops out of Italy and Spain.
The Trump administration has pointed to its dissatisfaction with key NATO allies, either reluctant or refusing any support for the U.S. on its strikes against Iran.
The Pentagon is expected to finalize a six-month review of the U.S. military presence in Europe by the end of the year, seeking to shift more defense responsibility to NATO countries.

sources.news_title: Why the U.S. Bomber Withdrawal From a U.K. Air Base Is Significant
sources.text:
President Donald Trump said Monday afternoon that "threats" had prompted the U.S. to remove all of its B-1 Air Force bombers from the RAF Fairford base in southern England over the weekend. The move came a week after several men were arrested nearby in relation to a suspected terror plot, which the U.K. government believes may be linked to Iran.
When asked if there was a specific threat that led to the bombers being moved, Trump told reporters: “Yeah, I think we can say that. They didn’t fly out by accident. A local farmer reported suspicious activity involving several men and white vans near the installation.
British counterterrorism officers arrested five men in their 20s on suspicion of preparing an act of terrorism and offenses under the Explosives Act.

RAF Fairford has supported American military operations for decades.
Its unusually long runway and infrastructure allow the base to accommodate the Air Force’s largest strategic aircraft, including the B-1, B-2, and B-52.
The base’s importance has grown during the war with Iran as the United States has relied on Fairford for long-range bomber missions.

sources.news_title: US removes bombers from UK base after suspected plot
sources.text:
(WASHINGTON) — The United States removed its heavy bombers from a base in the United Kingdom it had used to launch strikes on Iran, amid an investigation into a suspected plot to attack the base.
At least a dozen planes, including B-1 bombers, were redeployed to the United States from Royal Air Force Fairford, according to the Pentagon, which did not specify when or why the planes departed.
“While operational security precluded us from confirming the movement of our assets and forces in real-time, we can acknowledge now that all U.S. bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have re-deployed to their home stations in the United States,” a Defense Department official said in a statement on Sunday.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday morning that the aircraft redeployment reflects a “regular rotation” and that he “wouldn’t directly tie” the suspected plot regarding RAF Fairford to the action.
“[I]t’s not unusual to see rotations happen and movement of assets to different parts of the world based on exercises, redeployments, people changing out and new people coming in, new planes coming in, old planes going out,” Rubio said.
The Pentagon’s statement on the departure came after five men were arrested last month on terror charges near RAF Fairford.
They were arrested in possession of three vans in the village of Whelford, which is about 2 miles from the base, which hosts the U.S. Air Force and has since February been serving as a key hub for American operations against Iran — including for heavy bombers like the B-1.
The five were later released on bail after “extensive interviews,” authorities said.
The suspects, who have not been charged, “remain under investigation as we explore multiple lines of enquiry,” Laurence Taylor, head of National Counter Terrorism Policing in the United Kingdom, said on Sept. 28.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham told the BBC News in late September that there were “strong indications” that Iran “played a part in what happened.”
The Department of Defense said in its Sunday statement that the “U.S. Air Force bombers routinely operate around the world to support global force readiness and operational requirements.”
“The Airmen that operate America’s bomber force, including B-1s, B-2s, and B-52s, remain ready to deliver precision global strike capabilities – including through operations that launch and recover from the continental United States – anywhere, anytime,” the statement said.

sources.text:
The US has withdrawn its bombers from RAF Fairford over new security concerns.
The Pentagon confirmed on Sunday that the aircraft, stationed at the Gloucestershire base, were "redeployed to their home stations in the United States."
The move comes after six people were arrested in connection with a suspected terror plot targeting the base.
US officials told the New York Times the redeployment was ordered after more specific threat details emerged over the weekend.
A Pentagon official said the US Air Force bombers routinely operate globally to support force readiness and operational requirements.

"While operational security precluded us from confirming the movement of our assets and forces in real time, we can acknowledge now that all US bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have redeployed to their home stations in the United States," they said.
"The airmen that operate America's bomber force, including B-1s, B-2s, and B-52s, remain ready to deliver precision global strike capabilities — including through operations that launch and recover from the continental United States — anywhere, anytime."
The five British nationals, all in their mid-20s, who were arrested near the base on September 27, have been released on bail.
A sixth man, a 25-year-old dual UK-Iranian national, arrested on October 1, has also been released on bail.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said last week there were "strong indications" that Iran played a part in the incident.
Counter-terror police have said a quantity of petrol but no explosive devices were found in the vans that sparked the security alert.
Downing Street has insisted RAF Fairford is safe following the US withdrawal.
Asked on Monday whether the base was safe, the Prime Minister’s official spokesman said: "Yes."
He also pointed to comments by Defence Secretary Wes Streeting saying there were "tried and tested approaches to defend our bases around the country and throughout the world," but he declined to comment further on "foreign nations’ military operations."
The Liberal Democrats urged the Government to "get a grip" on security at military bases following the US withdrawal, saying the move raised "serious concerns about security standards."
Lib Dem defence spokesman James MacCleary said: "With three bases breached in the past year alone, this is not something the Defence Secretary, or the country, can afford to ignore."
RAF Fairford has been used in recent months by US bombers after former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer granted Washington permission to use British bases for "defensive" strikes against Tehran during the Middle East war.

sources.text:
An American B-1 Lancer bomber at RAF Fairford earlier this year. Photo / AFP
The withdrawal came with unusual speed, following what US officials said were threats of an Iran-based plot against the installation.
The United States rushed over the weekend to withdraw all 12 B-1 Air Force bombers from an air base in southern England after commanders received new threats about an Iran-backedplot against the installation, two US officials said on Sunday (Monday NZT).
The withdrawal was highly unusual. Such moves are rarely made so quickly from an allied air base in a peacetime country thousands of miles from a combat zone.
The need to move the bombers out of the base, RAF Fairford, was deemed so urgent that some of the planes and their flight crews left while aerial refuelling aircraft were still being scrambled to support their flights to the United States. At least three of the planes had landed at their home base in South Dakota by Sunday, the officials said, speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss operational matters.
The Pentagon’s European Command confirmed on Sunday that the bombers had left England but declined to comment on any new warnings.
“We can acknowledge now that all US bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford are redeploying to their home stations in the United States,” the command said in a statement. “US Air Force bombers routinely operate around the world to support global force readiness and operational requirements.”
The British Ministry of Defence declined to comment on the movements of US military assets.
US officials on Sunday declined to specify the nature of the new information that prompted the rapid withdrawal of the Air Force bombers, some of which had just arrived in the past week as part of a normal rotation of forces. One US official said the new information was part of the same threat warnings that surfaced three weeks ago, but specific details and a sense of urgency spiked in the past 24 hours, alarming commanders.
The sudden pullout of the bombers came a week after British police arrested five men who had been travelling last Sunday morning in white vans near the base, which has been used by US bombers in the US-Israeli war against Iran. The men were released on bail a day later after authorities did not discover explosives in the vans.
But police have repeatedly said the men remain under investigation, and a dual British-Iranian national was arrested on Thursday on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said last week that the British government believed Iran played a part in planning those events. US and British officials, as well as those in Germany and Israel, believe the operation is connected to Iran’s Revolutionary Guard or a separate military headquarters in Tehran. Iran has denied the accusations.
The episode has presented authorities with myriad puzzles as they try to sort out the events over the past week, including the arrests, the frantic evacuation of 85 homes, a bomb disposal robot searching the vans for explosives and a national security meeting convened by Burnham.
In July, Iran’s Revolutionary Guard issued a statement warning that allowing the United States to use the base “makes London responsible” for US actions. “Any base used to launch attacks on Iranian territory,” the statement said, “is a legitimate target for our forces.”
In September, US military commanders received a chilling warning from US and other Western intelligence agencies, according to American officials briefed on the information: RAF Fairford was the target of a potential Iran-backed attack.
The murky outlines of a plot had been pieced together through a combination of intercepted communications, informants and other intelligence. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said his intelligence officials also warned their British counterparts of a probable Iranian-sponsored attack, though they did not provide a specific target. Follow-up attacks were likely to include drones, the confidential assessments warned.
After that initial warning last month, concern among officials across Europe surged. According to a senior US official, Israel warned Germany that US bases there were at heightened risk, noting Spangdahlem and Ramstein in particular.
An Iran-backed plot to commit an attack in Britain would be a major escalation by Tehran against a Western country in apparent retaliation for the US-Israeli war against Iran.
